One-line judgment: chief executives are not about a senior title making the job easy; they determine and formulate policies and provide the overall direction of companies or private and public sector organizations within the guidelines set up by a board of directors or similar governing body, and plan, direct or coordinate operational activities at the highest level of management — the official duties are to 'Determine and formulate policies and provide overall direction of companies or private and public sector organizations within guidelines set up by a board of directors or similar governing body. Plan, direct, or coordinate operational activities at the highest level of management with the help of subordinate executives and staff managers'. In daily work they direct or coordinate the financial or budget activities of the organization to fund operations and maximise investments or improve efficiency (importance 88); confer with board members, organization officials or staff to discuss issues and coordinate activities or resolve problems (83); prepare budgets for approval, including those for funding or implementing programmes (83); direct and plan or implement the organization's policies, objectives or activities to ensure continuing operations and maximise returns on investment or increase productivity (81); prepare or present reports on activities, costs, budgets and government regulations or rulings (79); implement corrective action plans to solve organizational or departmental problems (79); analyse operations to evaluate performance of the company or staff in meeting objectives or to determine areas of potential cost reduction, process improvement or policy change (78); direct or coordinate activities of businesses or departments concerned with production, pricing, sales or distribution (78); direct human resources activities, including approving human resources plans, selecting senior personnel or establishing major departments (78); appoint department heads or managers and assign or delegate responsibilities (77); explain policies, rules, regulations or laws to organization, government or corporate officials or the public (77); review reports submitted by staff members to recommend approval or to suggest changes (77); negotiate or approve contracts and agreements with suppliers, distributors, federal or state agencies or other organizational entities (77); set the time period and define departmental responsibilities and coordinate the functions of departments and locations (75); and make presentations at meetings or conventions or write articles or present information to promote services and exchange ideas or accomplish goals (74). O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Five (extensive preparation needed), SVP range 8.0 and above, with an interest code of EC (Enterprising, Conventional); the occupation usually requires extensive experience and advanced management training, and most positions require more than five years of related experience. The core boundary is that this is a position responsible for the whole organization within the authorization granted by the governing body, and the consequences of decisions are borne by and constrained by the organization and the governance structure; this page does not present the Chinese mainland legal representative system or the management approach for state-owned enterprise leaders as a uniform threshold, nor does it present the U.S. occupational preparation description as a statutory qualification conclusion in other jurisdictions.

Signals to keep exploring: you are willing to make decisions in a high-uncertainty, high-responsibility environment and to get work done through others rather than personally; the O*NET work context shows that for this occupation 97% of respondents use email every day, 95% have a lot of freedom in how they make decisions, 92% have telephone conversations every day, 90% have face-to-face discussions every day, 90% work indoors in a controlled environment every day, 86% have a typical work week of more than 40 hours, 80% have a lot of freedom in determining tasks and priorities, 78% have very high responsibility for the work results of others, 67% are in continuous contact with others most of the time, 72% make decisions every day, 63% consider precision or accuracy extremely important, 55% have very high responsibility for the health and safety of others, 37% face time pressure every day, 28% experience conflict situations every day, 33% consider competition extremely high, 19% consider the consequences of error extremely serious and 26% very serious; the work of 19% is highly automated, 24% moderately automated and 39% not automated at all; 92% have a regular schedule. These figures show that most of the time is spent on decisions, communication and achieving results through others, that responsibility and pressure are real, and that they are constrained by the governance structure, authorization and records.

Conditions for pausing high investment first: you have not yet completed, under supervision, a full closed-loop exercise running from clarifying authorization and objectives to diagnosing problems and stakeholders to formulating options with budgets and metrics to driving execution and delegation to tracking results and correcting course to reviewing and reporting to the governing body; or you are unwilling to bear final responsibility, unwilling to decide when information is incomplete, or tend to avoid rather than handle conflict and compliance pressure through the proper procedure. And do not ignore authorization and compliance boundaries just because you want to manage: one of the important tasks of this occupation is to act within the framework set by the governing body and to implement corrective action plans. If you would rather be responsible for one function or professional line, general and operations managers and financial managers are adjacent positions with a different scope of authorization.

Qualifications and authorization must be checked separately: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Five (extensive preparation needed), SVP range 8.0 and above; the occupation usually requires extensive experience and accumulated management practice, and most positions require more than five years of related experience and postgraduate education. The O*NET education information describes U.S. occupational preparation and does not constitute a Chinese statutory qualification conclusion; before taking such a position, employer requirements, position training and the actual authorization should be checked separately. In Chinese mainland, the appointment and authority of the legal representative, company directors and senior management are determined by the Company Law, the articles of association and resolutions of the shareholders' meeting and the board of directors, and the leaders of state-owned enterprises have separate management authority and assessment rules, which must be confirmed under the applicable law and articles. This page does not extend the governance structure or qualification requirements of one jurisdiction to another, nor does it present industry association certification as a qualification for the position. Educational background, occupational certification, statutory and governance qualifications, and organizational authorization are four different things.

One line: this is a position that turns whether the direction is right, whether resources are allocated accurately, whether key people are being used, whether risks are isolated, and whether results can be examined by the governing body into reviewable evidence, producing strategy and annual operating objectives and budgets and investment decision records, organization and personnel appointment and authorization records, contract and agreement and compliance and risk control records, operating and performance and financial and risk reports, and external communication and relationship maintenance records; it is not a specialist execution role, does not replace the board of directors and the governing body's final decision power on major matters, and must not act beyond professional advice and organizational authorization.

Editorially organised from the O*NET tasks into three interconnected work fronts. The first is strategy and decisions: determining and formulating policies and objectives, analysing operations and markets to form strategy and annual operating plans, and making reviewable trade-offs when information is incomplete. The second is organization and people leadership: designing the organizational structure and authorization system, selecting, nominating or appointing senior and key positions within the authority, building team and performance mechanisms, and getting work done through guidance and motivation. The third is resources, compliance and external relations: preparing and approving budgets and investments, controlling resources and risks, handling contracts, regulations and governance communication, and maintaining relationships with the board, shareholders and external bodies. What the three have in common is that they speak through authorization, evidence and records; they differ in the scope and irreversibility of the decisions.
Setting direction within the authorized framework and allocating resources to key objectives

Read the authorization framework, governance requirements and prior results → diagnose the external environment, internal capability and key constraints → form objectives and strategic options and compare costs and risks → prepare budgets, metrics and responsibility allocation → drive execution and review at key milestones → review results and report and correct course with the governing body
Building and adjusting the organization and allocating responsibility and authority clearly

Make the responsibility boundaries, reporting relationships and authorization limits clear → select and appoint key positions and set objectives → build performance, incentive and development mechanisms → track progress and solve problems through meetings and reports → make and document adjustments when there is conflict or a person is mismatched → submit major personnel and authorization changes for decision under the rules

Propose or approve budgets within your authority, track cash flow and risk exposure, record deviations and drive correction. When compliance or safety anomalies occur, report promptly and take appropriate measures under the actual emergency procedure, professional judgment and authorization; do not write stopping or isolating all activities as a uniform operating authority.

Common adjacent positions include chief sustainability officers, general and operations managers, financial managers, sales managers, public relations managers and legislators. The key to boundary judgments is not the title but where the authorization comes from, what scope you are responsible for, who evaluates the results, and who holds the final decision power on major matters.
Setting organizational direction within the governance authorization and being responsible for overall results
The central output is organization-level decisions and resource allocation and results and governance communication records
Based on governance requirements and regulations and markets and internal data and budgets and performance indicators

General and operations managers may be responsible for the daily operations of multiple departments, multiple locations or even the whole organization and may take part in policy making; this occupation focuses on the highest level of management direction. Duties may overlap, and it cannot be judged from the title alone who manages only part of the business.
Strategic decisions, objectives and budgets, organization and personnel and authorization, performance and resource control, compliance and risk, and external relations and governance communication
Financial managers are responsible for the finance function and reporting; this occupation is responsible for overall resource allocation and operating results

Strategy and annual objectives and budget records, organization and appointment and authorization records, contract and compliance and risk control records, and operating and performance and risk reports
Sales and marketing managers are responsible for the market and sales lines; this occupation coordinates multiple lines and makes trade-offs under overall objectives

For major matters, the approving body must be checked item by item, and all investments, mergers or all executive pay cannot be assigned to the same kind of governing body.

U.S. BLS Table 1.2 lists the typical entry-level education for chief executives as a bachelor's degree, with related experience of 5 years or more and typical on-the-job training None; OOH emphasises years of management experience in a related field, and some large companies may require an MBA, while public sector positions have separate rules. The O*NET Job Zone Five/SVP8.0 and above is a general preparation level description; its education responses are master's 46%, bachelor's 32% and associate 5%, which is not a national recruitment share or a uniform postgraduate threshold.

Articles 74 and 126 of China's Company Law provide that the company manager is appointed and dismissed by the board of directors and exercises authority under the articles or as authorized by the board; the scope of senior management in Article 265 and the legal representative status in Article 10 are checked separately. The CEO title does not automatically equal director, manager, legal representative or chairman; a small company may lawfully have a single director exercise the powers of the board.

Six recurring occupational judgments: whether objectives and resources match; whether key positions and talent are in place; whether cash and risk are controllable; whether the decision information is trustworthy enough; whether compliance and governance procedures have been completed; and whether the results can be examined and explained by the governing body.
Judgment one: do objectives and resources match

First confirm whether the funds, people and time the objective requires are genuinely available, then decide whether the objective can be committed to; do not make commitments without resource support, nor leave the resource gap to be exposed only during execution.
Judgment two: are key positions and talent in place

For positions carrying key results, first confirm whether the person's ability, authorization and incentives match, then launch plans that depend on that position; adjust promptly and document where someone is not competent or not the right fit.
Judgment three: are cash and risk controllable

Suggested editorial checking: track cash flow, liabilities, guarantees and concentration; report anomalies promptly and assess the response according to available resources, payment obligations, statutory procedures and actual authorization, rather than substituting a vague isolation for specific financial and safety arrangements.
Judgment four: is the decision information trustworthy enough

Before key decisions, check the data source, framing and assumptions and require independent review where necessary; for data that clearly deviate from common sense or conflict with information from several sources, find out why before using it.
Judgment five: have compliance and governance procedures been completed

Submit major matters for decision under the articles and resolution procedures and keep records; where related-party transactions and conflicts of interest are involved, recuse and disclose under the rules, and do not skip governance procedures for the sake of efficiency.
Judgment six: can the results be examined by the governing body

Operating and risk reports should be able to answer objectives, inputs, outputs, deviations and corrections and keep the supporting data and decision basis so that the board, shareholders or competent department can review them, rather than giving conclusions only.

Within the framework set by a board of directors or similar governing body, chief executives determine and formulate policies and provide the overall direction of companies or private and public sector organizations, and plan, direct or coordinate operational activities at the highest level of management with the help of subordinate executives and department managers (O*NET-SOC 11-1011.00 official duties). In daily work they direct or coordinate the organization's financial or budget activities; confer with board members, organization officials or staff to discuss issues, coordinate activities or resolve problems; prepare budgets for approval; direct, plan or implement the organization's policies, objectives or activities; prepare or present reports on activities, costs, budgets and government regulations or rulings; implement corrective action plans to solve organizational or departmental problems; analyse operations to evaluate performance or to determine areas of potential cost reduction, process improvement or policy change; direct or coordinate activities of businesses or departments concerned with production, pricing, sales or distribution; direct human resources activities, including approving human resources plans, selecting senior personnel or establishing major departments; appoint department heads or managers and assign or delegate responsibilities; explain policies, rules, regulations or laws to organization, government or corporate officials or the public; review reports submitted by staff members to recommend approval or to suggest changes; negotiate or approve contracts and agreements with suppliers, distributors, federal or state agencies or other organizational entities; set the time period and define departmental responsibilities and coordinate the functions of departments and locations; make presentations at meetings or conventions, write articles or present information to promote services, exchange ideas or accomplish goals; serve on or chair governance bodies such as the board of directors and management committees; and possibly represent the organization externally or take part in legislative and policy discussions. Boundary of responsibility: the O*NET description covers U.S. top management tasks and is not an individual statutory authorization in China. Major investments, mergers and acquisitions, changes to the articles of association and remuneration matters must be checked separately against the law and the articles; the appointment and dismissal and authority of managers in China are in Articles 67, 74 and 126 of the Company Law, and investments and guarantees in Article 15. A CEO may concurrently be a director or manager, but the title does not automatically confer the corresponding statutory status.

paragraphs: The six directions share some capabilities with this occupation: goal setting and resource allocation, cross-department communication and negotiation, and performance and risk management. The real differences lie in the source of authority (a governing body, a professional line, or an electoral process), the object (the whole organization, one business or function, or public policy), and the responsibility (overall business results, line objectives, or public policy outcomes). When choosing, it is better to test with one deliverable business analysis or organizational plan than to compare titles.

The basis for comparison is the task and work activity descriptions on the O*NET-SOC 11-1011.00 page, the adjacent occupation list registered in this evidence route (chief-sustainability-officers, general-and-operations-managers, legislators, sales-managers, public-relations-managers) and the editorial notes on position boundaries; the entry, appointment and authorization of each position must be verified separately against its own page and the applicable jurisdiction's regulations and the organization's articles of association, and this table does not constitute any statutory duty or qualification requirement.

The table below compares positions and occupations adjacent to this occupation: General and Operations Managers, Financial Managers, Sales Managers, Public Relations Managers, Legislators, and Chief Sustainability Officers. The four columns each answer the same kind of question: what this direction does, where the key difference from this occupation lies, and what kind of person is better suited to choosing it.

General and operations managers run the operations of one business or function under an established strategy; this occupation is responsible for the whole organization's direction, resource allocation and results, and reports to the governing body.

People who want to do operations and execution within a defined line are suited to general and operations managers; people willing to be responsible for the whole organization's direction and results are suited to this occupation.
Responsible for the operations and performance of part of the business, a function or a region, with outputs mainly operational metrics and execution results.
General and Operations Managers

Financial managers are responsible for the finance function and reporting within a professional line; this occupation is responsible for overall resource allocation and business results, and uses finance as one input to decisions.
People who want to go deep into finance and compliance are suited to financial managers; people who want to make trade-offs and allocations under overall goals are suited to this occupation.
Responsible for the finance function, budgets, reporting, funding and compliance, with outputs mainly financial reports and funding arrangements.
Financial Managers
Sales managers are responsible for the goals of the marketing and sales line; this occupation coordinates sales, production, finance and other lines under overall goals and makes trade-offs.
People who like facing customers and the market directly are suited to sales managers; people willing to coordinate multiple objectives at the organizational level are suited to this occupation.
Responsible for sales targets, the team and customer relationships, with outputs mainly sales revenue and customer metrics.
Sales Managers

Public relations managers are responsible for reputation and communication within the communications line; this occupation represents the organization externally and is responsible for overall results, and the two have different scopes of authority.
People who want to focus on communication and relationships are suited to public relations managers; people willing to bear overall business responsibility are suited to this occupation.
Responsible for external communication, reputation and media relations, with outputs mainly communication impact and relationship maintenance.
Public Relations Managers

Legislators derive their authority from elections and the legislative process and are accountable for public policy and their constituency; this occupation derives its authority from a governing body (such as a board of directors and a shareholders' meeting) and is accountable for the organization's business results.
People who want to work in public policy are suited to the legislator direction; people who want to make business decisions inside an organization are suited to this occupation.
Influences public policy through legislation, budgets and oversight procedures, with outputs mainly bills, resolutions and public policy.
Legislators

Chief sustainability officers focus on sustainability topics, disclosure and related programs; this occupation covers overall strategy, operations and resource allocation, and sustainability is only one of its issue lines.
People who want to go deep into the sustainability specialty are suited to chief sustainability officers; people willing to be responsible for the whole business are suited to this occupation.
Responsible for sustainability strategy, disclosure and related risks and opportunities, with outputs mainly sustainability targets, disclosure and programs.
Chief Sustainability Officers

If you would rather be responsible for one business or function, you can further compare general and operations managers and financial managers; if you would rather face the market and customers directly, you can compare sales managers; if you want to work in public policy, you can compare legislators; if you want to go deep into sustainability topics, you can compare chief sustainability officers. These positions differ from this occupation in their sources of authority and responsibility structures, and the decision and resource judgments on this page should not be confused with professional-line or legislative authority.

Failing to complete the applicable governance and disclosure procedures may trigger regulatory, compensatory or other liability; this requires a legal basis, the elements of an offence, damage and a basis for duties, and it cannot be said that every missing procedure makes all individuals and the organization liable together.
